model_rationale: Counting array b[10000] is indexed by input values up to ~1e7; the first failing test crashes on that out-of-bounds write (UBSan index far past end). Undersized fixed array is the cause of the first failure.
Prints v[i+1] instead of v[i] after sorting: index arithmetic off by one (loop operator is right). Removing the +1 makes every test pass (repair-verified).

Builds the binary digits as a decimal int (bin, place *= 10); for inputs with >10 binary digits the int overflows (UBSan signed overflow). Small inputs pass, larger fail; int->long long fixes the first failing test.

The first scanf has 5 conversions for 6 values (and 6 pointers), so the second timestamp is read shifted (m2 becomes 2024) and the month loop runs past monthDays. Root cause is the input format string, not index/count arithmetic.

Uses truncation (int)c for floor/ceil, which is wrong for negative inputs, and prints the value with the wrong sign. The +-1 differences come from rounding semantics, not an off-by-one index or count.
The dual in-order merge recurses in the wrong order (emits a node before the smaller subtree of the other tree), producing a permutation. The +-1 deltas are swapped neighbours, not a loop bound.

int s[50] holds n values with n up to 100000; the first failing test (n=57) writes past s (ASan stack-buffer-overflow). The program has other bugs (scanf %s into ints, compares m not queries), but the first failure is the undersized fixed array.
Same submission family as cs-000701: s[50] for n up to 100000; the first failing test overflows s. Other bugs exist but the crash is the undersized array.

Ignores the input format (reads exactly 4 numbers with interactive prompts) and prints prompts, so every test fails on output. The number[i+1] read past the end exists but does not explain the first failure.
Same rounding error as cs-000530: (int)x truncates toward zero, so ceil/floor are wrong for negatives; sign of C printed wrong. Not index/count arithmetic.
Solves a different problem (checks whether the list is sorted) for the find-the-unique-number task. arr[i+1] past the end is incidental.

Reads and XORs num[15] (one past the end of num[15]) every iteration instead of num[i]. That is an out-of-bounds access exactly one past the end, which the taxonomy puts under OFF_BY_ONE rather than ARRAY_BOUNDS; it could also be read as a wrong-variable bug (OTHER). Needs a human call.

Loop runs i < n but reads arr[i+1], so the last comparison reads past the vector (bound should be n-1: count arithmetic, operator fine). That garbage comparison turns sorted inputs into 'Not Sorted'. Secondary issue: 'Acending'/'Decending' are misspelled, which would also fail.
Same as cs-001421 with the spelling fixed: i < n with arr[i+1] reads one past the end; the bound should be n-1. This explains the first failing test.

Prints the median of the initial list before processing queries; the expected output starts after the first insertion. Every line is shifted by one, so it looks like an extra token, but the cause is reading the output spec wrong, not a loop bound.
Same rounding error as cs-000530 (truncation used as floor/ceil for negatives, wrong sign for C).
Same rounding error as cs-000530 (float variant).
y*365*86400 does overflow int (UBSan), but both timestamps share the year so it cancels; the first failing test is wrong because every month is approximated as 30 days.
switch cases have no break, so ch1/ch2 always fall through to 365. The int overflow in y*365*86400 cancels between the two timestamps; the missing breaks cause the failure.

Builds the binary representation as a decimal int (x*10 + bit); inputs with more than ~10 binary digits overflow int (UBSan signed overflow, wrapped outputs). Small inputs pass; int->long long fixes the first failing test.
Same rounding error as cs-000530 (truncation used for floor/ceil of negatives).

Date-difference logic is wrong (days of the first month and hour/minute borrows are not handled), giving +1 in several fields. Not a loop-bound operator.

The rounding test n1+1-n >= n-n1 is inverted (rounds 90.22 up), and truncation is used for negatives. Removing a +1 happens to fix the first test, but the cause is the comparison logic, not count arithmetic.

i already points one past the last element, so 'i++; a[i]=c' skips a[n] and sorts an uninitialised slot into the list; the medians drift by one position. This is index arithmetic (store at a[i++]), not the loop-test operator.
Counting array array[15] is indexed by the input values (up to 32-bit ints); the first failing test writes far past the end (ASan stack-buffer-overflow, 3+ elements). Undersized fixed array.
Same as cs-002950: array[user[i]]++ with array[15] and values far above 15.
Computes ceil/floor as (int)(x+1) and (int)(x-1)+1, which is wrong for negatives and for the rounding choice. The +1 differences come from rounding logic, not count arithmetic.
if(a[i]=a[j]) assigns instead of compares; replacing = with == makes every test pass (repair-verified).

Two bugs: output has a leading space and a typo (' Descending )rder'), which already fails the FIRST test (presentation); and arr[100] is too small for n up to 1000, which crashes test 2. By the first-failing-test rule the primary is OTHER_ERROR with ARRAY_BOUNDS secondary; a rater may prefer ARRAY_BOUNDS since the presentation diff is cosmetic.

Already uses long long, but the binary digits of a 30-bit input read as a decimal number need ~30 digits, which overflows 64-bit too (wrapped negative output). Overflow of the integer type is the failure cause (fix needs a string).
